title: The Wine Room
excerpt: Workplace Romance · Forbidden Attraction · Slow Burn · Mature Romance
content:
By Friday, Naomi had developed a system.

She would arrive early, inspect the kitchen, review the reservations, and avoid looking toward the restaurant floor until absolutely necessary.

She would not drink the coffee Devraj left for her.

She would not smile when he remembered the smallest details about her day.

And she certainly would not think about the way he had stepped back beneath the pharmacy awning, leaving the decision entirely in her hands.

The system lasted until eleven forty-seven that night.

"Chef?"

Naomi looked up from her inventory sheet.

Devraj stood at the kitchen entrance holding a bottle of red wine.

"We have a problem."

"Is someone complaining?"

"Worse. The temperature-controlled wine room has decided it would rather be a sauna."

She put down her pen.

"How bad?"

"Bad enough that I need someone to approve moving the stock before we lose half the collection."

"Have you called maintenance?"

"They're on their way. I thought you should see it before we start moving anything."

Naomi followed him through the quiet restaurant.

The dining room had been cleared, its tables arranged for the next service. Candlelight reflected in the dark windows. The last of the staff were finishing their closing duties.

Devraj led her down a narrow corridor to the wine room.

Inside, rows of bottles rested in carefully labelled racks. The cooling system hummed unevenly overhead.

Naomi checked the temperature display.

"How long has it been like this?"

"About twenty minutes, according to the sensor."

"Why didn't you tell me earlier?"

"I did. You were threatening the pastry chef over a missing delivery."

"I was asking him a question."

"You were holding a whisk like a weapon."

She shot him a look.

He smiled.

For the next twenty minutes, they worked. Naomi helped him identify which bottles needed immediate relocation, while he recorded the inventory and contacted the supplier.

Their shoulders brushed occasionally in the narrow aisle.

Neither acknowledged it.

At last, Naomi stepped back and examined the remaining shelves.

"That should do it."

Devraj set down his clipboard.

"Thank you."

"Don't thank me. I don't want to explain to the owner why the wine collection smells like expensive vinegar."

"Still. Thank you."

She turned toward the door, but he was already there. He moved aside immediately, giving her room to pass.

It was such a small gesture.

It was becoming a problem that she noticed every one of them.

"Can I ask you something?" he said.

"You have a worrying habit of doing that."

"Why did you become a chef?"

The question caught her off guard.

She looked back at the shelves.

"My grandmother."

"Tell me."

"She cooked for everybody. Neighbours, cousins, strangers who turned up at the house because they'd heard there was food. She believed a good meal could make a terrible day bearable."

"Sounds like a good woman."

"She was."

Naomi smiled faintly.

"When she died, I started cooking seriously. I wanted to make something that could stay with people, even after they'd left the table."

Devraj was quiet for a moment.

"That's a beautiful reason."

"It's a practical one. People have to eat."

"And yet you remember every dish she made."

Naomi looked at him.

"How do you know that?"

"Because when you talk about food, you stop looking at the clock."

She had no answer.

For a few seconds, the room felt impossibly small.

Devraj rested his hand against the shelf beside him, careful not to touch her.

"Naomi, I want to ask you something else."

"Go on."

"Would you have dinner with me on your day off?"

Her heart gave a ridiculous little jump.

"We work together."

"I had noticed."

"You know my rule."

"I do."

"And you're still asking?"

"Yes. But I'm asking once. You can say no, and we can carry on working together exactly as we do now."

She looked at the floor.

A sensible answer was waiting for her. She could feel it. It was polished, familiar, and ready to protect her from the uncertainty of wanting someone.

But she was tired of rehearsing the same answer to every new possibility.

"One dinner," she said.

Devraj didn't move.

"One dinner?"

"Don't make me repeat myself."

His smile appeared slowly.

"Thursday?"

"Somewhere outside the restaurant."

"Obviously."

"And no wine lectures."

"That will be difficult. Wine is practically my personality."

She laughed.

He laughed with her.

Then the sound faded, and they were left looking at each other.

Naomi became aware of the space between them, the warmth of the room, the faint scent of cedar from the wine racks.

Devraj's expression grew serious.

"Can I kiss you?"

The question stole every clever response she had ever learned.

She looked at his mouth, then back into his eyes.

"Yes," she whispered.

He moved slowly enough for her to change her mind.

When he kissed her, it was gentle at first, a careful meeting of lips that seemed to ask another question.

Naomi answered by reaching for the front of his shirt.

The kiss deepened, and the weeks of restrained glances suddenly felt very long. She forgot the cooling system, the inventory sheets, and the rule taped above her kitchen pass.

For a moment, there was only the astonishing fact of him being there, kissing her as if he had nowhere else he would rather be.

Then a bottle shifted on the shelf behind them.

They broke apart, startled.

Naomi pressed a hand to her mouth.

Devraj looked at the bottle, then at her.

"That," he said, trying unsuccessfully to keep a straight face, "was an excellent demonstration of why wine storage requires proper supervision."

She laughed so hard she had to lean against the shelf.

"Get out."

"Gladly."

He opened the door for her.

They walked back toward the kitchen in silence, both smiling in ways they had no intention of explaining.

At the pass, Naomi stopped.

"Thursday," she reminded him.

"Thursday."

"And Devraj?"

He turned.

"What happened in the wine room stays in the wine room."

His smile softened.

"Of course."

She watched him disappear down the corridor.

Then she looked at the rule taped above her station.

For the first time, she wondered whether she had written it to keep her heart safe or to make sure nobody ever got close enough to prove that it didn't have to be afraid.
